    ctx user guide

    Getting started

    Install ctx

    Prepare your shell for a client workspace, then check that ctx can find the tools it needs.

    Install on your machine

    Run the full installer in a macOS or Linux terminal. On Windows, open a WSL2 Linux shell first. The installer sets up the CLI and shell integration. For a reproducible installation, use a release tag you have reviewed in place of main. 

    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Hei-Tech-Inc/ctx/v3.3.0/install.sh | bash

    Check your installation

    Open a fresh terminal so the shell loads the installed hook. The version command confirms which release is on your path. Doctor checks the shell hook, SSH include and integration tools. A machine with no client profiles can still run these checks. 

    ctx version
ctx doctor
    Next guide · Create a profile

    Getting started

    Create a profile

    Use one profile per client so Git, GitHub and your cloud tools use the intended identity.

    Choose an identity and folder

    Start the wizard and choose full setup. For this guide, use acme as the profile name. Supply your client Git name and email, and choose a dedicated work directory such as ~/clients/acme. Select the SSH key and cloud accounts that belong to the client. Review the paths and identities before confirming. 

    ctx setup

    Check the saved profile

    The dashboard shows the workspace, Git email, SSH key path and configured integrations together. Verify checks the profile’s paths and GitHub SSH authentication. A warning about a missing key can be expected if you skipped SSH setup. 

    ctx dashboard
ctx verify acme

    Start with Git only

    Choose clone-only setup if you just need a GitHub SSH alias today. Extend the same profile later when you know the workspace and cloud settings. 

    ctx setup --scope clone
ctx setup --extend acme
    Next guide · Switch workspaces

    Daily use

    Switch workspaces

    Use the current directory to select a profile, or activate one explicitly for a terminal session.

    Enter the client folder

    Change into the directory you selected during setup. At the next prompt, inspect the active profile. In a client repository, git config user.email should match the email in your dashboard. 

    cd ~/clients/acme
ctx status
echo "$CTX_ACTIVE_PROFILE"

    Switch manually

    Use the shell function installed by ctx to apply the profile variables to your current terminal. To see when automatic switching happens, enable transition messages. Clear a manual activation with deactivate. 

    ctx use acme
ctx config autoswitch-notify on
ctx deactivate

    Resolve a nested workspace

    When several clients share a repository, place a .ctx file containing profile=acme in the directory that belongs to that client. The nearest override takes precedence. Check the result from inside that directory. 

    ctx status --json
    Next guide · Clone with GitHub

    Daily use

    Clone with GitHub

    Route a clone through the client’s SSH alias and confirm the repository uses its Git identity.

    Clone into the workspace

    Replace ORG and REPO with a repository you can access. Start in the client folder. The profile option selects the GitHub SSH alias even if a different profile is active. 

    cd ~/clients/acme
ctx clone -p acme git@github.com:ORG/REPO.git

    Inspect the checkout

    Enter the new repository. Its origin should use github-acme for the SSH host. Compare the email with the profile before committing. Verify tests the client SSH connection. 

    cd REPO
git remote get-url origin
git config user.email
ctx verify acme

    Guard commits and pushes

    Install the Git guard if you want ctx to check the email on commit and the SSH alias on push. Check its status inside the repository because a repository-specific hooks path can take precedence. 

    ctx guard install
ctx guard status
    Next guide · Run commands and scripts

    Automation

    Run commands and scripts

    Give one process the client identity without switching every other terminal.

    Run with a named profile

    Put the program and its arguments after the double dash. The child inherits the profile’s Git identity, GitHub credentials and configured cloud variables. For kubectl, pass the intended context explicitly. 

    ctx run -p acme -- git var GIT_AUTHOR_IDENT
ctx run -p acme -- gh auth status

    Read structured checks

    Use list to enumerate profiles and status to inspect activation. Doctor emits machine-wide checks. Verify emits profile checks and returns status 1 on failure. For diagnostic results, inspect each check’s level and message. 

    ctx --json list
ctx --json status
ctx --json doctor
ctx --json verify acme

    Store a secret

    Set the value at the interactive prompt to avoid putting it in your command history. List shows key names. Processes launched with ctx run can receive the profile’s stored secrets, so select the child process deliberately. 

    ctx secret set acme API_TOKEN
ctx secret list acme
    Next guide · Troubleshoot activation

    Cloud accounts and clusters

    Activate a client workspace

    Configure cloud accounts during setup, or extend an existing profile. Activating it applies the configured AWS profile, Azure subscription, Google Cloud project and account, and kubectl context. Check the active context before working on a cluster.

    ctx setup --extend acme
ctx use acme
kubectl config current-context

    Run one cloud command

    Use a named profile to run the AWS CLI with that profile’s AWS environment. For a single kubectl process, supply the context explicitly. Replace acme-dev with the context from your own kubeconfig.

    ctx run -p acme -- aws sts get-caller-identity
ctx run -p acme -- kubectl --context acme-dev get namespaces

    Scripts and repository agent rules

    Scope a single process

    Run a tool with the profile’s Git author, SSH identity, GitHub credentials and configured cloud variables. Use the folder’s profile by default or pick one by name.

    ctx run -p acme -- git var GIT_AUTHOR_IDENT

    Give agents repository instructions

    Preview the instructions, then use --write in the repository to add the managed section to AGENTS.md. It tells agents how to check identity, scope credentialed commands and respond to a blocked commit.

    ctx agent-rules
ctx agent-rules --write

    Organize existing projects

    Development build. Check ctx help for the organize command.

    Find client repositories

    Scan the folders you choose. Review the GitHub owner or SSH alias alongside each suggestion. A personal fork may belong to a client project.

    ctx organize ~/work ~/Desktop/projects

    Adopt a checkout in place

    Choose an existing client profile, preview the assignment, then register the checkout. Repeat for each project. A local Git identity override takes precedence, so check the result in that repository.

    ctx --dry-run organize adopt acme ~/work/api
ctx organize adopt acme ~/work/api
cd ~/work/api
ctx explain

    Review keys and credential names

    List public SSH key fingerprints, profile references and SSH config declarations. Select an environment file explicitly to inventory its variable names. Values stay in that file.

    ctx organize ssh
ctx organize env-keys ~/work/api/.env

    Forget an assignment

    Remove a project's association before moving or reassigning it. After a move, supply its previous absolute path. Linked worktrees and submodules currently support inventory only.

    ctx organize forget acme ~/work/api

    Explain this terminal’s identity

    Requires ctx v3.3.0 or later. Check your installed version with ctx version.

    Check deployment targets

    Compare your current AWS account, Azure subscription, GCP project and Kubernetes context with the configured profile. The opt-in check reads the installed cloud CLIs. A mismatch or unverified target returns a nonzero exit. Project and context checks report local CLI selections.

    ctx explain --cloud

    Check the terminal you will use

    Run explain from the repository where you plan to work. Compare the folder’s profile with the active profile, the identity in this shell, and the Git email the profile expects. This is useful after switching clients in another terminal.

    ctx explain

    Investigate an unexpected email

    Git can take an email from repository configuration or from the shell environment. Inspect the configured source and the identities Git would actually use. After correcting the source, run the guard again in the same repository.

    git config --show-origin --get user.email
git var GIT_AUTHOR_IDENT
git var GIT_COMMITTER_IDENT
ctx guard check pre-commit

    Offboard a client

    Requires ctx v3.3.0 or later. Check your installed version with ctx version.

    Preview the handoff

    Use the profile name to print a read-only checklist at the end of a contract. Review the local cleanup and check for shared SSH keys. If another profile references the same key, coordinate its rotation before retiring it.

    ctx offboard acme

    Coordinate access revocation

    Agree with the client administrator which repository memberships, cloud permissions and cluster access to revoke. The administrator carries out those changes in the relevant providers. Confirm ownership of working copies, unpushed work and client notes before cleaning up locally.

    Remove the local profile

    Once the handoff is complete, run remove separately and review its confirmation. It removes the profile and its ctx-managed identity configuration and stored secrets. Review the workspace, SSH key files and mise.toml separately.

    ctx remove acme

    Dashboard and live checks

    Compare client profiles

    The dashboard shows each client’s workspace, active state, Git identity, SSH key path and configured integrations from saved profile metadata.

    ctx dashboard

    Verify one profile or diagnose the machine

    Use verify for a live SSH and GitHub identity check on one client. Use doctor to inspect installed tools, shell hooks and profile setup across the machine. Both commands support JSON for scripts.

    ctx verify acme
ctx doctor --json

    Repeatable setup and migration

    Preview a repeatable setup

    Prepare a KEY=value configuration using examples/setup.noninteractive.conf.example in the project repository. Preview the changes before applying the same configuration without prompts.

    ctx setup --config setup.conf --dry-run
ctx setup --config setup.conf -y

    Export on the old machine

    Export profiles, Git identities and ctx SSH host configuration to a directory. Transfer that directory to the new machine. Restore SSH keys and secret values separately.

    ctx config export ~/ctx-migration

    Import on the new machine

    Import the bundle from its new location, restore the credentials with your configured provider, and check that workspace paths and accounts match this machine.

    ctx config import ~/ctx-migration
ctx doctor
ctx verify acme

    Agent operations

    Kubernetes with MCP

    The local ctx MCP server gives an agent tools for one client’s clusters, namespaces, services, and runbooks. It uses ctx-core, the client’s login procedure, and the kubectl installed on the operator’s machine.

    Initialize client knowledge

    Inside your client workspace, create the knowledge directory. Edit clusters.yaml to describe login, environments.yaml to map names to a cluster and namespace, and services.yaml to map aliases to workloads. Recipes live in recipes/ and operator scripts in scripts/. 

    ctx knowledge init acme

    Register a local agent

    Choose the command for your MCP client. Start a new agent session in the client workspace. Folder scope determines the profile; outside a matching folder only client_context is offered. Adding a root that changes the client scope disables the session’s scoped tools and stops its port-forwards. 

    ctx mcp install claude
# Or, for Cursor:
ctx mcp install cursor

    Use a cluster password

    Store the value with the interactive secret prompt. List CLUSTER_PASSWORD under the cluster’s login.secrets and reference the variable in the operator-defined login command. For an existing kubeconfig login, specify both its path and context. 

    ctx secret set acme CLUSTER_PASSWORD

    Investigate a service

    Start with client_context. Use login, discover_services, logs, trace, describe_service and kubectl_read to investigate the selected environment. search_knowledge and get_recipe retrieve client guidance. activity shows earlier operations. For example, ask your agent to trace a request ID through two named services in staging.

    Approve a change

    restart, network_test, port_forward, kubectl_change, save_recipe, save_service and save_script ask for confirmation through the MCP host. Review the profile, environment, cluster, namespace and exact action. Protected environments require the canonical environment name. If the host cannot prompt, ctx returns a manual command and skips execution.

    Review what was recorded

    Inspect activity.jsonl and exports/ under the client knowledge directory. Configured profile and cluster login secret values are redacted in tool output and activity. Kubernetes Secret data and stringData are masked. Treat exported application logs as client data; applications can contain other sensitive content.

    Credentials

    Passwords and secret stores

    A profile records secret key names. The selected provider stores their values. Choose the provider before adding secrets so you know where credentials will be read and written.

    Choose a native provider

    auto selects the platform default. Keychain uses macOS Keychain. The file provider stores one file per key under ~/.ctx/secrets/<profile>/ with mode 0600; use disk encryption. The pass provider uses the Unix GPG password store at ctx/<profile>/<KEY>. Initialize pass with your own GPG identity before selecting it. 

    ctx config secret-provider pass
ctx doctor

    Set and inspect a key

    Enter the password at the prompt. list prints names; get prints the value and is best kept out of logs and recordings. For setup-managed injection, include the intended key name in the profile’s SECRET_KEYS. The cluster login can separately declare required keys in login.secrets. 

    ctx secret set acme CLUSTER_PASSWORD
ctx secret list acme

    Migrate a profile’s values

    Migration copies values between native providers on the machine. For example, copy from file storage into an initialized pass store, then select pass and verify the profile’s keys. The copy operation and provider selection are separate steps. 

    ctx secret migrate acme pass file
ctx config secret-provider pass
ctx secret list acme

    Move to another laptop

    Export/import carries profile and identity configuration. Restore secret values separately from your chosen provider, provision the required SSH keys, then verify the imported profile. 

    ctx config export ~/ctx-migration
# On the destination machine:
ctx config import ~/ctx-migration
ctx doctor

    Credentials

    Vault and 1Password

    Vault and 1Password can supply credentials alongside ctx. Native ctx storage choices are Keychain, file, and pass, with auto selecting a default. The Unix pass store is a separate product from 1Password.

    Use 1Password with a process

    Let ctx select the client identity and let the 1Password CLI resolve its own references. Prepare a local dotenv file containing references such as SERVICE_TOKEN=op://Client/Service/token and use the vault, item, and field names from your account. Replace your-command with your application. 

    ctx run -p acme -- op run --env-file=./references.env -- your-command

    Use HashiCorp Vault

    Authenticate to Vault using your team’s existing method. Vault Agent can render a restricted application configuration file, or a CI job can retrieve values for its child process. Run the application with ctx for its client identity. Avoid configuring the same variable in both sources so precedence is explicit.

    Understand reference handling

    Writing an op:// URI or a Vault path with ctx secret set stores that literal text. ctx does not authenticate to those services or resolve those references. Use the external tool for retrieval, rotation and audit. For ctx-managed Kubernetes logins, supply keys using a supported local provider.

    Hosted documentation

    Connect the documentation MCP

    Use the public Cloudflare endpoint to search this guide from an MCP client. The hosted service reads published documentation. Cluster login, client knowledge, credentials, and change approvals belong to the separate local ctx mcp server.

    Add the remote endpoint

    Choose a remote HTTP MCP server in your client and enter the URL below. In Claude Code you can register it with this command. No client profile or cluster password is needed. 

    claude mcp add --transport http ctx-docs https://ctx-workspace-guide.pages.dev/mcp

    Search or read a chapter

    Call search_guides with a query such as “Vault”, “trace”, or “SSH”. Use a returned chapter ID with read_guide to retrieve the complete guide. For example, read mcp for local operator setup or enterprise for external secret managers.

    Support

    Troubleshoot activation

    Work from the observed identity to the profile, shell hook or SSH setting that selected it.

    The shell shows the wrong client

    Compare the active profile, work directory and Git email. Check for a nearer .ctx override and for a manual activation. From the client repository, inspect which Git config file supplied the email. 

    ctx status
ctx dashboard
git config --show-origin --get user.email

    Changing directories does nothing

    Transition messages are off by default. Check the actual profile first. If the shell hook is missing, install it, open a new terminal and re-enter the client folder. 

    ctx doctor
ctx install-hook

    GitHub uses the wrong key

    Check the origin URL inside the checkout. A client clone uses the profile alias, such as github-acme. Doctor checks the SSH include and verify checks the profile key, alias and live authentication. 

    git remote -v
ctx doctor
ctx verify acme
